issues.issue: The quantity sold is "an amount set forth on the Mortgage Loan Schedule," but Exhibit B, where that schedule is to be attached, states only "Provided Upon Request." The subject matter of the sale cannot be identified from the instrument itself.

The Purchase Price turns entirely on the Purchase Price Percentage, which is "set forth in the Letter Agreement" between Morgan Stanley & Co. Incorporated and Bear, Stearns & Co. Inc. — neither a party here. The price cannot be computed from this Agreement alone.

The Purchaser takes principal from the Cut-off Date (June 1, 2007) but interest only "from and after the Closing Date," which the definitions fix as May 31, 2007 — a closing that precedes the cut-off. The allocation of the June interest and principal cannot be squared with those two dates.

This subsection assigns the Prior Purchase Agreements "except with respect to the Group 1 Mortgage Loans," yet Subsection 8.02 states flatly that the Purchaser "shall be the assignee of the representations and warranties of the related Originator ... as described in Subsection 6.01." Whether the Purchaser obtained originator recourse on Group 1 loans is left unresolved.

This subsection vests in the Purchaser "all rights arising out of the Mortgage Loans including ... all funds received by the Seller ... after the Cut-off Date," while Subsection 6.01 excludes the Servicing Rights from the conveyance and the definition of Servicing Rights captures late fees, Escrow Payments and amounts collected by the Seller. The same collections are allocated twice.

The paragraph ends in garbled and incomplete text — "and a asa a sale of assets 0 on the" — so the accounting-treatment covenant is cut off mid-sentence. What the Seller and Purchaser had to record cannot be read from the clause.

The final sentence puts all custodian fees on the Purchaser, while Section 11 allocates costs between the parties and puts "all other costs and expenses incurred in connection with the transfer and delivery" on the Purchaser subject to specified Seller items. The two cost provisions overlap without a stated priority.

The loans are said to be sold "on a servicing retained basis," yet the next paragraph requires the Seller to assign each Servicing Agreement to the Purchaser and to have the servicers service "for the Purchaser." What the Seller retained is not clear from the two paragraphs read together.

The paragraph directs the reader to "the Mortgage Loan Schedule attached as Exhibit C," but the Mortgage Loan Schedule is defined and attached as Exhibit B, and Exhibit C is the schedule of Prior Purchase and Servicing Agreements. Which document identifies the governing servicing arrangement is uncertain.

The sentence duplicates its verb — "No consent ... is required for the transactions ... from any court ... having jurisdiction over the Seller is required" — leaving the warranty ungrammatical. Its scope is blurred by the doubled construction.

The warranty is framed as a double negative — the Seller "does not believe, nor does it have any reason or cause to believe, that it cannot perform" — so what state of affairs is warranted is hard to pin down. It gives no objective standard of ability to perform.

The Purchaser is made assignee of the Originators' Representations and Warranties "as described in Subsection 6.01," but Subsection 6.01 expressly excludes the Prior Purchase Agreements for Group 1 Mortgage Loans from the assignment. The two provisions describe different assignments.

The sentence runs "within 120 days of the earlier of either discovery by or receipt of notice by the Seller of the breach ... the Seller shall take such actions as described in the following paragraph," with conditions (1) and (2) embedded so that the subject and the 120-day period cannot be cleanly matched. Whether the 120 days is a cure window or a deadline to act is not clear on the face of it.

The paragraph states overlapping and inconsistent triggers: the Seller must cure and "if such breach cannot be cured" repurchase at the Purchaser's option, but the next sentence gives a 120-day cure period and the third a 180-day substitution window keyed to the Closing Date. Which timetable governs a given breach cannot be read off the words.

The indemnity is available only "provided the Mortgage Loans are not the subject of a Reconstitution," yet Section 12 exists precisely to effect a Reconstitution of these loans into a securitization, which would extinguish the indemnity the same clause then calls part of the Purchaser's "sole remedies." The two provisions cannot comfortably be read together.

The clause fixes when a cause of action "shall accrue" — on discovery or notice plus failure to cure or repurchase — which may be read as a condition precedent to suit or as an attempt to postpone the limitations period. That choice decides timeliness and is not resolved by the words.

Accrual here is triggered by "discovery of such breach by the Purchaser or the Servicer or notice thereof by the Seller," while the Subsection 8.02 trigger paragraph runs from "discovery by or receipt of notice by the Seller." The two paragraphs identify different discovering parties for the same breach.

"FPD" is defined in Section 1 as "first payment default provisions ... as described in Subsection 8.03," but this subsection describes no such provisions and instead points onward to the Prior Purchase Agreements. The definition is circular and the triggering default event is never stated.

This section speaks of a single "Closing Date" while the immediately following conditions and Section 10 refer to "each Closing Date" and to "the initial Closing Date," contemplating multiple closings. Whether more than one closing was possible turns on which reading prevails.

The enumeration is scrambled — the markers "(iv)" and "(v)" appear in the middle of clause (iii) and their text follows afterwards — so the closing conditions cannot be matched to their numbers as printed. The list also closes with an open-ended condition that "all other terms and conditions of this Agreement (unless waived) shall have been complied with."

The list of closing documents is numbered "1." and then simply runs on without numbers for the remaining four items, so the enumeration is broken. The set of required originals must be inferred from the run-on text.

This paragraph contemplates a Reconstitution "on one or more dates (each, a 'Reconstitution Date')" of "some or all" of the loans, while the next paragraph limits the Purchaser to a single Reconstitution. The two sentences pull against each other.

This caps the Purchaser at "one (1) Reconstitution," but Section 18 states that "the Purchaser shall be limited to three (3) assignments or transfers with respect to the Mortgage Loans and this Agreement as described in Section 12." The two limits on the same transfers are irreconcilable.

This paragraph obliges the Seller to repurchase or substitute "as if it were the related Originator" whenever an Originator fails to remedy a breach, without the 120-day machinery or the "sole remedies" limit of Subsection 8.02. Whether the Subsection 8.02 conditions and remedy cap apply to this backstop is unresolved.

The closing sentence declares all of the Purchaser's rights and remedies "distinct from, and cumulative with, any other rights or remedies ... afforded by law or equity," while Subsection 8.02 states that cure, substitution, repurchase and indemnity "constitute the sole remedies of the Purchaser" for warranty breaches. The two remedy provisions directly contradict each other.

The section insists the transaction is a true sale and not a debt instrument, while Section 13 has the Seller grant the Purchaser "a lien on and a continuing security interest in each Mortgage Loan" and hold the loans in custody. A court asked to characterise the transfer would have to reconcile the two.

This section limits the Purchaser to "three (3) assignments or transfers with respect to the Mortgage Loans and this Agreement as described in Section 12," but Section 12 limits the Purchaser to one Reconstitution. The permitted number of transfers is stated twice and differently.

The covenant turns on what it is to "solicit a Mortgagor ... for the purpose of refinancing," a term the section never defines and whose boundary is then cut back by two carve-outs. Whether particular marketing crosses the line is the classic question this wording leaves open.

Exception (i) reads "so long as such promotional material either is sent to the mortgagors for all of the mortgages in the servicing portfolio ..." — the word "either" has no matching alternative, so one limb of the safe harbour is missing. The scope of the permitted advertising cannot be determined.
